theme: I do not rebuke you for sacrifices
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 50. You read this psalm in Unit 6. This time read it as a prophet’s sermon, with the books of Kings in mind, and ask what God is saying to a people that went through the motions of religion but lived in injustice.
settingTheScene: Psalm 50 is a psalm of Asaph, the temple musician. It presents God as a judge who summons his people to court. You first read it in Unit 6 as part of the story of worship. Here, in the age of the prophets, it takes on a different weight. This is exactly the charge that Amos, Hosea, and Micah will bring: sacrifices without obedience, religion without righteousness. Hosea 6:6, the anchor verse of this unit, could be a summary of the psalm.
observation: “The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (v. 1).
“Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth” (v. 2).
“Hear, O my people, and I will speak, O Israel, I will testify against you” (v. 7).
“I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before me” (v. 8).
“For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills” (v. 10).
“If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (v. 12).
“Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High, and call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (vv. 14-15).
“These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself” (v. 21).
interpretation:
The scene is a courtroom, and God is both judge and witness. He summons the whole earth to listen, but the case is against his own people. The covenant people are on trial. This is the language of the prophets: God has a case against Israel.

The surprising part is the charge. God does not say, “You have failed to offer sacrifices.” He says, “I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices.” They have kept the rituals. The problem is that they think the rituals are what God needs. He answers with one of the Bible’s great statements of divine self-sufficiency: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine.” God does not depend on offerings. He owns every animal. To treat sacrifice as a way of feeding or bribing God is to misunderstand who he is.

What he wants is thanksgiving, vows kept, and prayer: “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.” The real sacrifice is a heart that gives thanks. The relationship is not transactional. “Call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” He is the giver, and we are the receivers. Our part is gratitude and trust.

The second half of the psalm turns on the wicked, those who recite God’s statutes but hate discipline. They steal, commit adultery, and slander, while keeping up the appearance of religion. They thought God’s silence meant approval: “You thought that I was one like yourself.” The great danger of religious hypocrisy is the assumption that God is like us, that he overlooks what we overlook.

The psalm ends with a warning and a promise. “Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart.” But “the one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God.”
connection: Hosea 6:6, which Jesus quotes in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, says, “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice.” Hebrews 13:15 says, “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God.” Acts 17:24-25 says that God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything. Jesus confronted those who honored God with their lips while their hearts were far from him (Matthew 15:8).
application:
Ask if you ever treat your religious activity as a way of earning God’s favor.

Offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving today: name five things you are grateful for.

Examine whether any part of your life is hidden behind religious appearance.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you can offer him a sacrifice of thanksgiving.
Ask him to keep you from hypocrisy.
Call on him in your day of trouble.
